correctness.rationale: The complete-color classification uses disjoint color sets across r nonempty parts with only r+1 colors. In the monochromatic case no blank vertex can see r colors. In the split case no split-part blank can be forced, and at most one nonsplit part may be seedless; conversely those exact conditions explicitly force every blank. Disjoint combinatorial counting gives the whole seed polynomial, probability polynomial and minimum coefficient. The provided standalone enumerator independently checked all 9,213,533 partial assignments in 34 profiles with no discrepancies. This is a universal mathematical proof, not an extrapolation from finite checks.

originality.rationale: Farr (2026) defines and studies the graph invariant, including selected small examples and two-color cases, but its inspected definitions/examples and main results do not state the exact r>=3 one-spare-color complete multipartite enumeration. The published max-degree-two three-color formula and earlier complete-bipartite arbitrary-palette formula address r=2 or degree<=2, neither dominating all r>=3 cases. A known exact chromatic-palette multipartite forcing formula has lambda=r rather than r+1 and lacks the unique-surjective-split construction. The theorem compares statements, not titles: it creates a different color-usage regime and proves necessity and sufficiency. Targeted published-finding corpus and open literature searches found no covering theorem. Residual risk from alternative terminology and unindexed publications remains.
residual_risks: Search and partial full-text inspection cannot exclude an equivalent theorem in uninspected passages, an unindexed preprint, or a work using an alternative term for this forcing process.
The known bipartite arbitrary-palette and multipartite exact-palette boundary cases are prior work and excluded from the novelty claim.

value.rationale: Farr's newly introduced forced-coloring graph polynomial motivates determining exact probabilities and distributions for natural graph classes. The one-color surplus above chromatic number is a canonical first boundary where a previously monochromatic color class can split; the theorem discovers that such a split class must be entirely seeded and that only one other class may lack a seed. This structural rigidity is not a parameter renaming of the lambda=r or bipartite cases. The formula determines all coefficients, the exact forcing probability and minimum seed counts for arbitrarily many nonempty parts and arbitrarily large part sizes, and supplies concrete analytic test cases for the general invariant. It does not purport to solve all palettes.
